newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Fukui no stranger to environmental danger.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Fukui no stranger to environmental danger.

text.p: Japan's Fukui Prefecture, where the fisheries and tourism industries face disaster as oil spilled from a sunken Russian tanker laps up on its scenic coastline, is no stranger to environmental danger.

The predominantly rural prefecture, nestled between steep, snow-capped mountains hiding ancient but still active Zen Buddhist temples and the rugged coast of the Sea of Japan, bears the brunt of Japan's ambitious nuclear power programme.
Fifteen reactors, the world's densest concentration of nuclear plants, ring the Wakasa Bay area in the south of the prefecture.

The relatively obscure Fukui unwillingly made world headlines in December 1995 when Japan's prototype fast-breeder reactor, called Monju, was shut down after leaking two tonnes of non-radioactive liquid sodium.
The accident caused no harm to the environment, but forced the indefinite closure of the plant and galvanised opposition to Japan's aims to steadily increase nuclear power capacity.

Although the sale of nuclear energy to the populous Osaka region to the south is a key source of prefectural income, opposition among Fukui residents has grown and spread to nearby prefectures in a region prone to earthquakes.

Citizens of Fukui, whose low population density and cost of living and high education standards win it high marks in surveys of Japan's most livable regions, have also long lived with debris shed by the increasing number of ships plying the busy Sea of Japan between Japan and Russia and the two Koreas.
The looming oil pollution disaster has forced fishermen along vast areas of Fukui's Echizen coast to ponder the loss of a season -- or many seasons -- of lucrative crab and shrimp fishing.
A delicacy that draws thousands of tourists to Echizen each year, a single large Echizen crab can command 10,000 yen ($85).
Oil from the tanker has so far hit shore along 100 km (60 miles) stretching from Kyoto Prefecture to Fukui, whose coast is dotted with fish farms, fishing ports and tourist resorts.
On Tuesday, before the final extent of damage was known, one fisheries official said the annual 30 million yen ($260,000) income harvested from the relatively small port of Mikuni was in jeapardy.
"This is a tragedy," taxi driver Mikio Inoue said as he surveyed the oil-soaked coast. "Now is the best season for fish when the water is cold."
